content.text: The OWASP Top 10 ranks the most critical risk categories for web applications, so developers know where to look first. OWASP calls it an awareness document and, used as a standard, "the bare minimum": several of its risks can't be tested by tools, and business logic isn't on any list. For a checklist you can verify, use the OWASP ASVS, and threat-model the flows that move money or data.

A deal needs a security questionnaire, and one question reads "Is your application OWASP Top 10 compliant?" The team runs a scanner, gets a clean report with a green "OWASP Top 10" badge, and answers yes. Two weeks later, finance flags a customer who was refunded three times for one order. The cancel endpoint required a login, checked that the order was hers, used EF Core and ran over HTTPS. It never checked whether the order was already cancelled, and no scanner rule knows that a cancelled order can't be refunded again.
The common misconception
The belief: the OWASP Top 10 is the security checklist for web apps. Cover each of the ten items, or get a tool report that says you did, and the app is secure.

It's an easy belief to hold, because the list has earned its reputation. The 2025 edition, OWASP's eighth, is built from testing data on over 2.8 million applications plus a survey of practitioners. Contracts and questionnaires ask for it by name, and security tools advertise coverage of it. OWASP itself notes that organizations have used it "as a de facto industry AppSec standard since its inception in 2003." When everyone treats a list as the bar, clearing it feels like being done.
What actually happens
It's an awareness document, by design

OWASP is explicit about what the list is for: "The OWASP Top Ten lists are awareness documents, meant to bring awareness to the most critical risks of whichever topic they cover. They are not meant to be a complete list, only a starting place." And if you use it as a coding or testing standard anyway, "know that it is the bare minimum and just a starting point."
Here is the 2025 list, as OWASP publishes it:

items.text: A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures
A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures

content.text: Each item is a category, not a test
Every entry groups many weaknesses, each catalogued as a
CWE

. The 2025 edition maps 248 CWEs into its ten categories, out of 968 in MITRE's dictionary. Some of them a tool can find; many it can't. OWASP spells out the difficulty: "we document AppSec risks, and not necessarily easily testable issues." Its own example is A06 Insecure Design, which "is beyond the scope of most forms of testing."

The refund bug is a design flaw. The A06 page describes this exact gap: "flaws in the business logic of an application, e.g. the lack of defining unwanted or unexpected state changes inside an application." It also explains why careful coding can't save you later: "An insecure design cannot be fixed by a perfect implementation as needed security controls were never created to defend against specific attacks."
The ranking looks backward

OWASP picks eight of the ten categories from contributed data and two from the community survey, because "examining the contributed data is essentially looking into the past." A new kind of weakness takes years to reach automated tests at scale, so the data always lags. And ten slots leave real risks out: OWASP ranked twelve categories from the data, then kept eight of them.
No tool covers it

Scanners match patterns they know: a query built from strings, a missing header, an outdated package. They can't know that an order may be cancelled once. OWASP is blunt about it: "Tools cannot comprehensively detect, test, or protect against the OWASP Top 10 due to the nature of several of the OWASP Top 10 risks."
The bug no scanner flags

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: Both versions pass the same scan. The fix is one rule about state, and it only exists because someone asked "what transitions must never happen?" That question is
threat modeling

, and the A06 page recommends using it for "authentication, access control, business logic, and key flows", backed by tests built from "use-cases and misuse-cases": cancel twice, cancel two times in parallel, cancel a shipped order.
OWASP also publishes its own guidance on when the Top 10 fits and when you need a real standard. A selection of its rows:
The
ASVS

is the checklist the Top 10 is mistaken for. OWASP recommends it to "anyone wanting to adopt an application security standard", because "it's designed to be verifiable and tested." Version 5.0.0, published in May 2025, defines three levels. Level 1 "contains the minimum requirements to consider when securing an application", and about Level 2 the standard says: "Most applications should be striving to achieve this level of security." Every requirement must end in a "pass" or "fail" decision, which is exactly what a questionnaire answer needs.

blocks.title: "Full Top 10 coverage" is a red flag

content.text: OWASP says it plainly: "OWASP discourages any claims of full coverage of the OWASP Top 10, because it's simply untrue." A clean scanner report means the tool found none of the patterns it looks for. It says nothing about your business rules or about the risks no tool can test.

blocks.title: Answer the questionnaire with what you verified

content.text: Instead of "yes, Top 10 compliant", write what's true: which ASVS level you verify against, which requirements are open, and which flows you threat-model. It's a more honest answer, and a stronger one.

OWASP describes two new categories and one consolidation: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures expands 2021's Vulnerable and Outdated Components, A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions is new, and Server-Side Request Forgery was rolled into A01 Broken Access Control.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Use the Top 10 for awareness and training

content.text: Give every developer the 2025 list and the "How to prevent" section of each category. That's the entry-level training OWASP rates it for.

items.title: Pick an ASVS level as your real checklist

content.text: Start with Level 1, aim for Level 2, and record each requirement as pass, fail or not applicable. Review the list when the app changes.

items.title: Threat-model the flows that move money or data

content.text: For checkout, refunds, sign-up, password reset and permissions, list the states each flow can be in and the transitions that must never happen.
Cancel twice, cancel in parallel, refund more than was paid, skip a step in a wizard. Each one should fail, and a test should prove it.

items.title: Keep the scanners, drop the badge

content.text: Static and dynamic scanners still catch real bugs such as injection. Just don't let their report stand in for the parts they can't see.
Key takeaways

items.text: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document; used as a standard, OWASP calls it "the bare minimum".
Each item is a category of many weaknesses, and some, like insecure design, can't be found by tools.
No tool covers the whole list, and OWASP calls claims of full coverage untrue.
Use the OWASP ASVS as your verifiable checklist: start at Level 1 and aim for Level 2.
Threat-model and test your business rules, because that's where scanners are blind.
